The graph of $y={f}^{′}(x),$ the derivative of $f(x),$ is shown above. Given that $f(0)=0,$ which of the following could be the graph of $y=f(x)?$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that critical points of $y=f(x)$ occur when ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(x)$ does not exist. In our case, there are three critical points: 

$\,$ $x=-3,$ $x=-2,\,$ and $\,x=-1.$

Also, we have the following: 

- If ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ then $f(x)$ is increasing.

- If ${f}^{′}(x)<0$ then $f(x)$ is decreasing.

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,-3)$ | $-3$ | $(-3,-2)$ | $-2$ | $(-2,-1)$ | $-1$ | $(-1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |
| $f$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ |

Let's now sketch the graph of $y=f(x):$

- First, we draw the critical points. Consider the vertical lines $x=-3,$ $x=-2,$ and $x=-1.$

- Since we are told that $f(0)=0,$ we can draw that point on the graph.

- Since $f(x)$ is increasing $↗$ on $(-1,0)$, the point at $x=-1$ must be below the $x$-axis.

- Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $↘$ on $(-2,-1)$, the point at $x=-2$ must be higher than the point at $x=-1.$

- Since $f(x)$ is increasing $↗$ on $(-3,-2)$, the point at $x=-3$ must be lower than the point at $x=-2.$

So, we draw it as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/66296cbca22d3059fba111935808d1bb0a78e9de31c45948fce207d998c9cfd2.png)

- Next, we consider the behavior of $y=f(x)$ in the neighborhood of the critical points:

- Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $↘$ on $(-\infty ,-3)$ and increasing $↗$ on $(-3,-2)$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ goes up to the left and to the right of $x=-3.$

- Since $f(x)$ is increasing $↗$ on $(-3,-2)$ and decreasing $↘$ on $(-2,-1)$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ goes down to the left and to the right of $x=-2.$

- Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $↘$ on $(-2,-1)$ and increasing $↗$ on $(-1,\infty )$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ goes up to the left and to the right of $x=-1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/b26af4cdc5af02f2cf0a9a0092f0fe908d70acd428e6a1e24bc848bcc99125e4.png)

- Finally, by connecting and extending the existing parts with a smooth curve, we obtain a possible graph of $y=f(x):$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/938c86a415620a2e80873f7cee72b2ebaf5579ae2e67eb966bb1f8836e62c087.png)
